explanation: Fires on a finite auxiliary right after a sentence subject, strongest for perfect-tense auxiliaries that predict 'been' or a past participle (English 'has/have', especially 'There has been'/'It has been', French 'a/ont/avait', Spanish 'ha'). A second strong use is 'under' in license boilerplate ('Licensed under the Apache License', 'modify it under the terms'). Other modals and copulas after a subject ('will', 'would', 'should', 'is', 'were') fire moderately, and other tokens barely fire.

Fires on the modal 'would' or contracted ''d' after a subject, strongest in hypothetical or polite uses such as 'How would you...', 'What would be...', 'I would like...', 'She would have been...'. Other auxiliaries or verbs right after a subject ('is', 'were', 'says', 'do you') fire only weakly to moderately.

Fires weakly and diffusely on nouns naming technical objects, inputs or components in software, electronics or patent-style text ('text' in textfile, 'checkbox', 'laser', 'image', 'device', 'signal', 'button', '(Bundle'). It is strongest when the noun is the object of an action such as 'from a', 'controlled by' or 'click the'. Some unrelated function words and math tokens also activate, so the pattern is loose.

A mixture of several things: (1) 'even' after a negation ('never even', 'don't even', 'hadn't even', 'Not even'); (2) a fraction or percentage after a small number ('1 percent', '2%', 'a fourth of', 'nine of 10'); (3) the 'pone' subword in PLOS-style citation keys ('[@pone.0...'); and (4) assorted boilerplate tokens in legal headers and URLs.

Fires on verbs, prepositions and pronouns in the middle of narrative or conversational clauses, with a slight preference for 'asked'/'ask' and prepositions after a verb ('appearance on', 'playing with', 'working with', 'attention on'). There is no clear defining feature, so it is hard to predict.

Two unrelated triggers. (1) 'of' after a compass direction in geographic location phrases ('south-east of', '10 miles west of', 'northwest of Downtown Ottawa'). (2) Inner or final subword pieces of uncommon proper names, mostly surnames ('Zel[az]ny', 'Fare[se]', 'Feg[ely]', 'Ey[re]', 'Hux[ley]').

Strongest on 'to' or 'particularly' in the patent boilerplate 'The present invention relates to X, and more particularly/specifically to Y'. It also fires fairly strongly on assorted subword tokens inside compound words, names and code identifiers ('result[_of]', 'pref[abric]ated', 'Y[itz]chak', 'surface[-mount]able') with no common thread.

A mixture: (1) continuation subwords inside biomedical and technical terms ('syn[ov]ial', 'interfer[on]', 'end[ob]ronchial', 'pup[ation]', 're[per]fusion', 'mi[RN]As', 'turbo[fan]'); (2) speech-report verbs after 'he' in quotes ('he yelled', 'he told', 'he added'); (3) assorted code and legal tokens ('in' in Ruby stack traces, '{ get;', 'United States').

Fires on content words, often technical or computing vocabulary, inside non-English text. It is strongest in Chinese ('文本', '编译', '访问') and also fires on Japanese, Russian, Spanish and French nouns ('стандарт', 'проект', 'electrónico', 'développement'). English tokens fire only weakly, apart from 'of' in 'one of the'.

Fires on the first subword piece of a new segment inside identifiers, URLs, slugs, CSS class names, file paths, handles and hex codes, typically right after a hyphen, slash, dot or '#' ('-p' in 'supporter-poll', 'python3-pip', 'ruby-1.9.3-p385'; '/F'; '.ph'; '-con'). It also fires on mid-word pieces of Dutch and Portuguese words. It is weak on ordinary English prose.

Fires on a scattered mix of tokens: 'to' in 'in addition to', 'write' in the GPL 'if not, write to the Free Software', 'though'/'if' after 'even', digits of patient counts or years in medical abstracts, 'public' in Java code, and expansions of acronyms. These share no clear common feature.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of tokens in boilerplate, code, citation and technical-name contexts ('commission' in affiliate disclaimers, 'pp.,' in book citations, 'Password=' in connection strings, 'Jobs' in 'Tax Cuts and Jobs Act', 'e.g', 'Closure', bracket and colon tokens in docs or error messages). No single concept predicts it.
